== Introduction ==

* [[:Category: Ballynasollus Townland, Derryloran and Kildress Parishes, County Tyrone]]
* [[:Category: Muntober Townland, Kildress Parish, County Tyrone]]

We limit it to early 19th century to keep this page manageable.

== Unsolved mysteries / unattached clues ==
* John Glasgow(senior) 1898 has a Will Calendar entry but no civil registration death record. Wife Martha dies in 1894 (has newspaper obituary
** [https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/details-civil/d8a1733202971 Their marriage] - John is son of Henry Glasgow, wife Matilda Little.
* Who is the father of [[Glasgow-1647|David]] (b. 1836) - name James.
* [[Glasgow-2265|Maude Glasgow (abt.1876-1955)]] is a mystery. The wiki article (and a Mid-Ulster Mail piece) says her father was Silas Glasgow of Killycurragh and she was born 1876. However, [[Glasgow-1697|Silas Ebenezer Glasgow (abt.1825-1875)]] died 1875 and I have found no suggestion of any other Silas Glasgow. Nor do there seem to be any compatible posthumous birth records to his wife.  There is [[Glasgow-1972|Silas William Glasgow (1844-1913)]] but he is claimed to marry in the US in 1870.
* [https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/details-civil/1df5627598500 1869] William child of William & Jane McCartland of Ballynagilly. We don't have them yet.

== Family-letter household: William, James and Samuel ==

The research question is whether the letter’s named sons can identify the later Killycurragh households. The maintained reading of PRONI T1959/3 describes the writer’s paternal grandfather William Glasgow of Killycurragh and his wife, an unidentified Miss Cunningham of Omagh. Their sons included James and Samuel, who remained on the family farm; Samuel occupied the parental house. The writer’s father was the minister who died in July 1801. This is an undated, unsigned family recollection known through a published transcription, not an original newly inspected in this review. An earlier HTTP 403 check failed; the published transcription was subsequently read in the browser on 20 October 2026. The original letter remains uninspected.

Prefer the William named in PRONI T1959/3 as James Glasgow-4145’s probable working father, at 82% confidence. The letter’s paternal uncle James lived and died on the Killycurragh farm, matching the name, specific locality, generation and deceased status of the probate subject indexed at Killycarragh on 21 March 1836. The letter supplies the parent relationship absent from that index. The whole match remains inferred because the original probate document is lost and the letter is derivative; another local James remains possible.

Prefer the William named in PRONI T1959/3 as Samuel Glasgow-1698’s probable working father, at 66% confidence. The positive case combines the expressly named Samuel in the letter, the exact Killycurragh family-farm setting, and the later Samuel’s documented farmer/probate household there in 1857. It replaces an unnecessary blanket hold with a testable family placement. The identity is less secure than James’s: there is no traced lease succession or age for the letter’s Samuel, and the current birth estimate may represent a later generation.

The percentages assess each entire father-to-profile proposition, including identification of the named son with the later profile; they are subjective comparative judgments, not measured frequencies. The original letter and holding succession remain unverified. Samuel’s circa-1800 birth is an estimate, and a materially older Samuel or a later same-name descendant is possible. His wife Anne’s approximate 1801 birth and their children in the 1820s–1830s do not date Samuel himself. A nephew or later tenant could share the name and townland. Do not transfer a recorded relationship to a later adult merely from the letter’s parent clause. William’s birth and death remain unknown. The full letter now supplies an older William as his father; the Scottish profile candidate is possible at 36%. His mother remains unidentified. Miss Cunningham is retained as William’s reported wife, without selecting her as either profile’s mother. No existing person is merged or redated, and no live WikiTree edit has been made.

Inspect PRONI T1959/3 and associated family papers; test William’s identity against existing candidates and trace the Killycurragh holding through leases, rentals and valuation revisions. Establish Samuel’s age independently. The 1836 index date is probate information, not James’s exact death date.

== Two William generations and the Coleraine couple — 20 October 2026 ==

The full published transcription is now accessible in the browser; the earlier HTTP403 is an access history, not a continuing source block. The question is how the letter’s two parental lines connect the later Killycurragh family with the existing Moneymore accounts.

The freshly read published transcription of PRONI T1959/3 distinguishes an older William of Killycurragh, the writer’s paternal great-grandfather, from his son William, the writer’s paternal grandfather and husband of Miss Cunningham. The younger William is the Cunningham husband, whose sons included James and Samuel. His son John married Margaret Glasgow after ordination at Coleraine and died at his father’s house in Orritor in July 1801. The surviving child, the anonymous writer, was born five months later; Margaret died in 1817. The separate church compilation identifies John Glasgow from Orritor, ordained at New Row, Coleraine, on 8 March 1796 and dead on 13 July 1801. The shared ministry, origin, name and death month strongly identify the husband. The writer separately describes Margaret’s father William as a son of James Glasgow and Margaret Rutherford; the two parental lines must not be collapsed into one grandfather.

Select the letter-defined William of Killycurragh as Rev. John Glasgow’s father at 94% (strongly supported). The writer explicitly gives the writer’s father John, the writer’s paternal grandfather William and his Cunningham marriage. John’s Coleraine ordination, Orritor origin and July 1801 death match the separate New Row minister entry. This concerns the minister’s record-defined identity; it does not identify his grandfather with a Scottish baptism or upgrade his brothers’ later-profile matches.

Select [[Glasgow-1318|William Glasgow]] as the possible father of the letter-defined Cunningham husband at 36%. The letter supplies an older Killycurragh William, son of the Tullycoll/Tullyall William and brother of James (husband of Margaret Rutherford) and John (husband of Anne Mason). The 1705 Kirknewton child William has a named father William and a generation compatible with being grandfather of the minister ordained in 1796. The 1702 John baptism supplies a compatible second named son in that Scottish father cluster; the existing James-1025 family supplies the Irish James comparison. This is a positive but non-exclusive family-cluster hypothesis. The Scottish child’s adult identity and migration remain unproved. The 36% includes that identity uncertainty; it is not a confident Scottish–Irish bridge.

Select [[Glasgow-2426|William Glasgow]] as Margaret Glasgow’s probable father at 84%. That profile represents William, son of [[Glasgow-1025|James Glasgow]] and Margaret Rutherford, which matches the letter’s maternal-grandfather family position. The letter explicitly names the eldest daughter Margaret as the minister’s wife and the writer’s mother. The profile’s circa-1735 birth and circa-1829 United States death are inherited claims, not exclusionary records and not corrected here. The letter calls William an eldest son; the circa-1735 estimate conflicts with the earlier estimated births of his attached brothers. Those unverified estimates require checking and are preserved here. This is the maternal grandfather, distinct from the Cunningham husband. Original records and an independent adult-life bridge remain to be found.

Reassess [[Glasgow-1025|James Glasgow]]’s existing [[Glasgow-1026|William Walter Glasgow]] father hypothesis from 12% to 32% (possible). The newly read full family-letter sequence explicitly supplies James, husband of Margaret Rutherford, as a son of the Tullycoll/Tullyall William, with brothers John and William. This adds a named father role and a three-son comparison to the compatible Kirknewton William/John baptisms. It supports testing that household more than chronology alone did. The letter-defined Irish father has not been identified with the Kirknewton adult, and the James profile’s estimated generation and 1759 Drumcarn probate identity remain unproved. No independent migration or property bridge has been found. The old 12% assessment and its sources remain in the history; no live father attachment is changed.

These are exact subjective assessments of complete relationship-and-identity propositions, not measured probabilities. The family letter is undated and unsigned and is read through Albert Rutherford’s published transcription of a photocopy, not an inspected PRONI original. The minister list is a derivative compilation whose independence from the family tradition is unproved. The Scottish adult identities remain possible: neither the letter nor the 1705 baptism supplies a migration, occupation, property or witness bridge between Kirknewton and Tyrone. The letter’s three-son family and second-cousin statement are internally consistent clues from one source, not independent corroborations. Existing people, vital fields and mothers are preserved. Miss Cunningham and Anne Rutherford are reported maternal names, not transferred to existing maternal profiles. The letter’s first-settler story is family tradition, not proof of the first Glasgow in Tyrone or of the surname’s origin.

== Four sons in the Irish recollection,24October2026 ==

Father James-1025, specifically the James/Margaret Rutherford family-account role: James-1024 18%→78%, Samuel-1492 23%→76%, Robert-2425 18%→77%, William-2426 46%→84%, all now probable. The American Robert-12/Arthur-649/Joseph-1543 father grades remain35%, John-4027 remains30%, Mary-4030 remains22%; James-1025’s own William-1026 father remains32%.

The anonymous family recollection printed by Faris on p.9 explicitly gives James Glasgow, husband of Margaret Rutherford, four sons: William, Robert, James who settled near Moneymore, and Samuel who went to America, plus daughter Ellen. The letter-defined father is the family role represented by James-1025. These are specific named relationships, substantially stronger than the contributed-tree and locality summaries used by the earlier percentages. The same full-letter tradition was already read on 20 October; actual Faris pages now confirm its full structure. Its reproduction by Albert Rutherford and Faris’s pedigree are dependent presentations, not independent witnesses.

These are probable, not confident, relationships reconstructed from an anonymous retrospective family recollection, with no newly inspected parent register. The original letter remains uninspected. Faris calls the anonymous recollection file5 within PRONI T1959, while Rutherford’s reproduced copy cites T1959/3; retain this reference discrepancy pending archive checking. The 1759 probate index says Drumcarn and names no kin; neither that testator nor the inherited life dates are identified by this reassessment. The letter calls William eldest although the imported sibling birth estimates put him later; those estimates remain unverified. Faris also flags Samuel’s infant daughter and surviving mother-in-law in1824 against the supposed early paternal death. Those tensions require testing, not automatic exclusion. Preserve all existing people, vital fields, maternal grades and alternatives. No Scottish migration, identity merge, live edit or new father attachment is claimed.

[https://glasgow.phenotype.dev/branches/research-irish-moneymore/#irish-four-sons Complete four-son comparison] · [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CS3J-H9VW-J Faris,printed pp8–9].


== William and Nancy Glendinning: the 1903 family account ==

The research question is whether the named household can identify the later adults, and whether it supplies any earlier Glasgow connection. The 1903 memorial calls Nancy the elder’s fifth daughter, born in April 1803, and names her mother Mary Bell. It says she married [[Glasgow-1675|William Glasgow]] of Killycorragh, a farmer and businessman, and explicitly lists the eight children above. It records Nancy’s death at Belle Center on 20 March 1890, aged 87.<ref>Unsigned, A Brief Memorial of the Deceased Members of the Glendinning Family, from the Siege of Derry to the Present Time (1903), [https://glendinning.name/history/irish_glendinning.pdf#page=17 PDF p.17], “Glasgow–Glendinning Family”; no printed page number. Cover and complete paragraph visually checked 24 October 2026.</ref>

The named family and the existing individual records support these father assessments: [[Glasgow-3158|Mary]] 88→97%, [[Glasgow-3146|Matilda]] 83→92%, [[Glasgow-2825|Alexander Fleming]] 85→95%, [[Glasgow-3150|Benjamin]] 84→88% and [[Glasgow-3147|Jane]] 82→86%. The first three are now confident; Benjamin and Jane remain probable. These strengthen existing attachments. [[Glasgow-3151|Adam]] remains 77% because the adult identity and 1834/1840 birth claims are unresolved; Henry Cunningham and Isaac Watts remain 92%. The book supplies neither child birth dates nor an interleaved birth order, and its WikiTree Space reproduction is not an independent witness.

William’s own father remains unknown and unrated. This Ohio ruling elder is not identified with the London/Hull physician in the T1959 family letter. No parent is attached from shared Killycurragh residence. [https://glasgow.phenotype.dev/branches/research-irish-derryloran/#glendinning-family-confidence Current catalogue-linked family study].
